appraisal_events.evidence: In his study of the last twenty years' politics for the Revue des Deux Mondes the prince speaks of M. de Norpois "dans les termes les plus flatteurs"; Norpois calls on him, thanks him, and says he does not know how to express his gratitude. The prince meanwhile thinks: "Ce n'est pas encore celle-ci", like a man trying another key in a lock.
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois is publicly honoured in print by a prince and courted as the man who holds the door of the Institut; the narration immediately reduces the homage to a key tried in a lock.

appraisal_events.evidence: Behind the ceremony, his own thoughts: "Sapristi, ces gaillards-là me laisseront crever avant de me faire entrer. Dépêchons", and, of the Institut, that dying before election "serait vraiment désagréable".
appraisal_events.explanation: The free indirect access to his mind strips the courtly manner down to impatient calculation and fear of dying uncrowned, and the passage means that exposure.

appraisal_events.evidence: At the Opéra he turns his request into a favour granted — "ce n'était pas une demande ... mais une offre" — and presents her as a person for whom his wife and the grande-duchesse Jean feel, "sans la connaître", a great admiration, worth offering to their guests at a dinner for the king and queen of England; her house is "un pareil bureau d'esprit", access to which would console him for renouncing the Institut.
appraisal_events.explanation: Spoken before Norpois, who listens "avec une affabilité souriante", the speech raises Mme de Villeparisis into a rare and sought-after figure — while the reader sees the admiration invented on the spot as the price of an introduction.

status_effects.explanation: A prince flatters him in print and comes to him as the indispensable intermediary; the deference is public and acknowledged on both sides.
The narrator's exposure of his inner haste and lock-picking makes his elaborate delicacy look like machinery.
In the exchange itself he has the upper hand: he converts a petition into an offer, and Norpois — no mean judge — esteems his tact and settles in to listen.
Inside the world of the passage she is spoken of as a prize: sought by a princess and a grande-duchesse, fit to be shown to the king and queen of England, admitted to only by favour.

ambiguities: The elevation of Mme de Villeparisis is voiced entirely by a man engineering an introduction, so it is impossible to say from the passage how much of her reported rarity is real and how much is the currency he has chosen to pay in.
